newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Germany, invigorated by G7, restates jobs goal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Germany, invigorated by G7, restates jobs goal.

text.p: Germany is drawing new vigor to attack structural problems at home in talks with leaders of the Group of Seven nations and is determined to stick by its goal of halving unemployment.

Economics minister Guenter Rexrodt on Saturday told reporters that the summit talks here between G7 leaders, finance ministers and foreign ministers, "have given us strength domestically to pursue structural reforms."
Germany is grappling at home with the urgent need to reform its highly regulated labor market to make companies more competitive and reduce near-record unemployment.
Progress on the wide-ranging reforms -- set to emcompass pensions and taxes as well as labour market rigidities -- has been slow in consensus-driven Germany.
Unions and to some extent industry are reluctant to abandon established practices which constitute the German economic model.
But there is growing urgency to ensure that Germany remains competitive internationally with German unemployment now running at near-record levels of about 11 percent or nearly 4-1/2 million people.

Political leaders at the G7 talks had been expected to exchange ideas on ways to tackle unemployment, particularly in view of the success of the United States and Britain in reducing their jobless queues.
The G7 also includes Canada, France, Italy and Japan.

Questioned at the briefing about the German government's chances of meeting its stated goal of halving unemployment by the year 2000, Rexrodt said there could be no question of Bonn abandoning the goal, although many say it is not achievable.

"This is a goal which has been set jointly by the government, the trade unions and industry...It is a goal, and an ambitious goal. And we are continuing to strive for it. It would be a poor show if we were to abandon it," he said.
Yet the aim of halving Germany's 4-1/2 million unemployed in the next three years has been labelled unrealistic by independent economists.
Germany's IFO research institute said last week that the jobless queues could only be cut to meet the target if the German economy grew by 5.75 percent per year over the next three years.
Bonn is predicting economic growth of no more than 2.5 percent this year.

Turning to the general agenda for the G7 talks, Rexrodt said he expected trade and economic issues to be at the center of the discussions in Denver, even if they had not received a high billing on the official agenda.
"Economic and trade issues are at the center of the conference. The problems in Africa, for example, also have a strong link to these issues," he said.

Looking at the overall economic situation, Rexrodt said the G7 countries were keen to maintain inflation-free growth in the long term, making use of increased globalization to give new vigor to the world economy.
"The current position is that globalization is being seen by all as the driving force for more growth. That means enormous opportunities," he said.
"What we want is sustainable inflation-free growth accompanied by stability policies and structural reform where it is needed...as well as open markets," Rexrodt said.
